glossary.Observation: Documenting student behavior/performance in the natural setting.
glossary.Interview: Gathering information directly from teachers, caregivers, or the student.
glossary.Portfolio: A collection of student work analyzed across time.
glossary.Anecdotal record: Dated narrative notes describing specific incidents, behaviors, or interactions.
glossary.Scaled checklist: Predetermined behaviors/skills rated by frequency, intensity, or degree.
glossary.Formative: Assessment used during learning to provide feedback and guide instructional adjustments.
glossary.Summative: Assessment used after a period of learning to evaluate achievement, often connected to a final grade.
glossary.Norm-referenced: Interprets performance relative to a comparison group.
glossary.Criterion-referenced: Interprets performance against defined standards or mastery criteria.
glossary.Progress monitoring: Frequent, ongoing measurement used to evaluate student response and growth.
glossary.Validity: Degree to which an assessment measures the intended construct for its intended use.
glossary.Relevance: Degree to which the information directly addresses the concern or decision at hand.
glossary.Bias: Systematic unfairness or construct-irrelevant barriers that disadvantage a group.
glossary.Duration: The time span or repeated observation/testing period emphasized in a data set or course scenario.
glossary.MTSS: Multi-Tiered System of Supports; a broader framework integrating academic, behavioral, and social-emotional supports.
glossary.RTI: Response to Intervention; evaluates how a learner responds to evidence-based intervention.
glossary.SEL: Social-emotional learning; includes self-awareness and responsible decision-making.
glossary.PBIS: Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports; a framework for proactive behavior support.
glossary.FERPA: Federal law protecting education records and related parent/eligible-student access rights.
glossary.ADA: Civil-rights law protecting people with disabilities from discrimination and supporting equal access.
glossary.IDEA: Federal special education law governing evaluation, eligibility, IEPs, FAPE, and procedural protections.
glossary.Rowley: Supreme Court case associated with FAPE and individualized educational benefit in special education.

questionBank.clue: Suspected disability + documented lack of progress → formal evaluation referral.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Eliminate options that are true in general but do not answer the exact question being asked.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Rowley → individualized educational benefit. Persistent lack of progress despite appropriate intervention → referral indicator.

questionBank.prompt: A reading test produces stable scores across three administrations. However, English learners score lower mainly because several passages rely on unfamiliar U.S. idioms unrelated to the reading skill being evaluated. Which TWO concerns are strongest?
questionBank.why: The cultural/linguistic barrier creates unfairness (bias) and introduces construct-irrelevant language demands that threaten whether the test measures the intended reading skill (validity).
questionBank.clue: Hard questions may legitimately involve more than one quality concept—identify the PRIMARY mechanisms.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Do not treat validity, relevance, and reliability as synonyms. Ask whether the issue is construct accuracy, fit to this concern, or consistency.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Measures intended construct → validity. Directly addresses this concern/decision → relevance.

questionBank.prompt: A teacher observes a student during math, interviews the caregiver, reviews six weeks of work samples, and graphs weekly computation probes. Why is this stronger than relying on one standardized score?
options: It triangulates qualitative and quantitative evidence across methods and time
It guarantees eligibility for special education
It eliminates the need to consider bias
questionBank.answer: It triangulates qualitative and quantitative evidence across methods and time
questionBank.why: Multiple measures provide converging evidence and reduce dependence on the limitations of any single tool.
questionBank.clue: Look for MULTIPLE SOURCES + DIFFERENT METHODS + TIME.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Eliminate options that are true in general but do not answer the exact question being asked.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Numbers/counts/scores → quantitative. Descriptions/perspectives/context → qualitative.

questionBank.prompt: A team has strong behavior data but weak academic data, yet the initial concern includes both behavior and reading. What is the best next step?
options: Assess the scope and depth of existing data and collect targeted academic information
Discard the behavior data because it is not academic
Refer immediately without addressing the missing academic evidence
Repeat every assessment with a different administrator
questionBank.answer: Assess the scope and depth of existing data and collect targeted academic information
questionBank.why: The data set should adequately address the full concern. Existing evidence is reviewed first, then missing relevant data are collected.
questionBank.clue: Coverage matters: does the evidence address ALL parts of the concern?
questionBank.distractorCoach: Eliminate options that are true in general but do not answer the exact question being asked.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Follow the sequence: concern → gather information → team → plan → implement → evaluate/review.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best reflects the educational principle associated with Rowley in the context of this course?
options: Interventions and individualized programming must be designed to provide educational benefit
The school must maximize each student’s potential to the greatest possible degree
The IEP must guarantee grade-level academic performance
Students with similar disability labels should receive substantially identical services
questionBank.answer: Interventions and individualized programming must be designed to provide educational benefit
questionBank.why: Your pre-assessment keyed Rowley to individualized supports designed to confer educational benefit, not a behavior-specific rule.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Eliminate options that are true in general but do not answer the exact question being asked.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Rowley → individualized educational benefit. Persistent lack of progress despite appropriate intervention → referral indicator.

questionBank.prompt: An IAT already has several test scores but still does not know how a student approaches independent work in the general classroom. Which additional source would best fill that gap?
questionBank.why: Direct observation adds contextual evidence about how the student actually behaves and performs during classroom tasks.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Another formal score may be valid information, but it does not answer the missing contextual question.
questionBank.keyClue: When the missing information is what actually happens in the classroom, think observation.

questionBank.prompt: A team wants to understand why a student avoids reading aloud. They already have classroom observations and work samples. Which additional assessment method would add the student's own perspective?
questionBank.why: An interview can gather the student's explanation, perceptions, and experiences that are not visible in work samples or observation alone.
questionBank.distractorCoach: A scaled checklist can rate behavior, but it does not necessarily explain the student's own reasoning or experience.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Ask which source can provide a perspective that cannot be directly observed.

questionBank.prompt: A pre-referral file contains weekly accuracy percentages, a frequency count of call-outs, teacher narrative notes, and a caregiver interview. Which statement best describes the evidence?
options: It combines quantitative and qualitative data
questionBank.answer: It combines quantitative and qualitative data
questionBank.why: Percentages and counts are quantitative, while narrative notes and interview responses are qualitative. Using both can provide performance data and context.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Do not classify the entire file from just one source; mixed evidence can contain both numerical and descriptive data.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Separate the type of data from the assessment method: numbers and descriptions can appear in the same file.

questionBank.prompt: A reading report states that a student mastered 9 of 12 grade-level skills and also scored at the 38th percentile nationally. Which interpretation is accurate?
options: The report contains both criterion-referenced and norm-referenced information
The percentile makes the mastery result invalid
questionBank.answer: The report contains both criterion-referenced and norm-referenced information
questionBank.why: Mastery of defined skills is criterion-referenced information, while percentile rank compares performance with a norm group.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Do not assume the whole assessment must use only one interpretation when the report explicitly provides both.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: One report can contain two different reference frames; ask what each score is compared against.

questionBank.prompt: A teacher gives a reading probe every Friday for eight weeks and graphs each result against the student's goal. What makes this progress monitoring rather than a one-time benchmark?
options: The repeated measurements show change over time
The probe is given on Friday
questionBank.answer: The repeated measurements show change over time
questionBank.why: Progress monitoring depends on repeated, ongoing measurement so a team can evaluate growth and intervention response.
questionBank.distractorCoach: A numerical score alone does not make an assessment progress monitoring.
questionBank.keyClue: Ongoing + repeated + trend over time are the central clues.

questionBank.prompt: A student starts an intervention at 42% accuracy and reaches 44%, 43%, 45%, 44%, and 46% over five checks while the goal is 70%. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: Growth is minimal and the intervention should be reviewed
Continue the intervention unchanged because the scores show an upward trend
Increase intensity immediately because the current score remains below the goal
Extend monitoring before making any change because five checks may not establish a stable pattern
questionBank.answer: Growth is minimal and the intervention should be reviewed
questionBank.why: The repeated data show little movement toward the goal. The team should review the intervention and relevant implementation evidence rather than treat the pattern as automatic eligibility.
questionBank.distractorCoach: A small increase can sound positive, but adequate response requires meaningful progress toward the target.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Judge the trend against the goal, not whether the final score is slightly higher than baseline.

questionBank.prompt: Which situation would make progress-monitoring results difficult to interpret even though data were collected weekly?
options: Administration procedures changed from week to week
questionBank.answer: Administration procedures changed from week to week
questionBank.why: Changing administration procedures can introduce inconsistency, making score changes harder to attribute to student progress.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Frequency of measurement does not compensate for unreliable administration.
questionBank.keyClue: Repeated data are only useful when measurement conditions are sufficiently consistent.

questionBank.prompt: A team has six weeks of stable progress-monitoring data showing improvement that closely approaches the goal. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Continue the effective support while monitoring progress
Reduce the support because the student is approaching the goal
Increase intervention intensity so the student reaches the goal faster
Move to less frequent monitoring because the data are stable
questionBank.answer: Continue the effective support while monitoring progress
questionBank.why: When data show an adequate response, continuing the successful intervention while monitoring is more defensible than treating referral as automatic.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Referral is not the goal of MTSS; the goal is effective support based on data.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Progress monitoring informs decisions in both directions: lack of response may prompt review, while adequate response supports continuation.

questionBank.prompt: Why is a baseline score useful but insufficient by itself for evaluating an intervention?
options: It establishes a starting point but does not show a trend
It shows initial severity but does not indicate how the student responds to intervention
It can be compared with a benchmark but does not show implementation fidelity
It describes current performance but does not establish whether later change is instructionally meaningful
questionBank.answer: It establishes a starting point but does not show a trend
questionBank.why: Baseline provides the point of comparison. Repeated measures after intervention are needed to determine whether performance changes over time.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Do not confuse having a starting score with actually monitoring change.
questionBank.keyClue: Baseline = starting point; progress monitoring = repeated evidence after that point.

questionBank.prompt: A team has documented a reading concern and reviewed existing data. What should happen before the intervention is implemented?
options: The team should meet and develop a specific plan
The team should collect additional data before discussing an intervention plan
The intervention should begin immediately and the formal plan can be written after the first progress check
The student should be referred for a comprehensive evaluation before the team selects a targeted intervention
questionBank.answer: The team should meet and develop a specific plan
questionBank.why: After information gathering, stakeholders discuss the evidence and develop the intervention plan before implementation.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Several choices may describe legitimate school actions; choose the one that fits the current step and evidence.
questionBank.keyClue: Identify where the team is in the process and what evidence the decision requires.

questionBank.prompt: A student receives targeted intervention with fidelity, but progress-monitoring data remain flat across six weeks. Which action best reflects data-based pre-referral decision-making?
options: Review effectiveness and consider adjustment or referral based on the full evidence
Increase intervention intensity while continuing the same progress-monitoring schedule
Collect additional diagnostic data before making any change to the intervention
Extend the intervention cycle to establish a longer trend before considering another action
questionBank.answer: Review effectiveness and consider adjustment or referral based on the full evidence
questionBank.why: Evaluation and review use response data to determine whether support should continue, change, or lead toward referral.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Several choices may describe legitimate school actions; choose the one that fits the current step and evidence.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Identify where the team is in the process and what evidence the decision requires.

questionBank.prompt: Which evidence set gives an IAT the strongest basis for deciding whether additional data are needed?
options: Recent assessments, observations, intervention data, and stakeholder information tied to the concern
Only the most recent test score
questionBank.answer: Recent assessments, observations, intervention data, and stakeholder information tied to the concern
questionBank.why: The team should examine the scope and depth of relevant existing data before deciding what gaps remain.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Several choices may describe legitimate school actions; choose the one that fits the current step and evidence.
questionBank.keyClue: Identify where the team is in the process and what evidence the decision requires.

questionBank.prompt: An intervention plan exists, but the teacher has not yet started it. Which statement is accurate?
options: The team is still in plan development, not implementation
The team is already in evaluation and review
The team is in initial concern
questionBank.answer: The team is still in plan development, not implementation
questionBank.why: Implementation begins when the agreed intervention is actually delivered.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Several choices may describe legitimate school actions; choose the one that fits the current step and evidence.
questionBank.keyClue: Identify where the team is in the process and what evidence the decision requires.

questionBank.prompt: A team sees a large gap between expected and actual performance and also has weekly data showing little response to intervention. Which statement is strongest?
options: Both discrepancy and RTI information may be relevant to the decision
The two forms of evidence contradict each other by definition
questionBank.answer: Both discrepancy and RTI information may be relevant to the decision
questionBank.why: A performance gap and response-to-intervention data answer different questions and can both inform a comprehensive decision.
questionBank.distractorCoach: Several choices may describe legitimate school actions; choose the one that fits the current step and evidence.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Identify where the team is in the process and what evidence the decision requires.

questionBank.prompt: A behavior measure produces stable ratings across three administrations, but its items do not address the anxiety concern named in the referral. Which combination is most accurate?
options: Validity is strong because scores are stable
questionBank.why: Stable scores support reliability, but poor alignment with the intended concern raises validity and/or relevance concerns.
questionBank.distractorCoach: The trap is choosing a quality term that is true in general but not the main problem in this scenario.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Separate reliability, validity, relevance, bias, and duration before deciding which issue is primary.

questionBank.prompt: Two evaluators disagree sharply when using the same subjective rating criteria. The items themselves clearly address the intended construct. Which concern is primary?
questionBank.why: The construct may be appropriate, but inconsistent ratings across evaluators point first to reliability.
questionBank.distractorCoach: The trap is choosing a quality term that is true in general but not the main problem in this scenario.
questionBank.keyClue: Separate reliability, validity, relevance, bias, and duration before deciding which issue is primary.

questionBank.prompt: An assessment accurately measures decoding, but the referral question concerns broad reading comprehension. What should the team question first?
options: Relevance of the measure to the referral concern
Reliability because the test is narrow
Bias because decoding is different from comprehension
Duration because the test is brief
questionBank.answer: Relevance of the measure to the referral concern
questionBank.why: A valid measure for one skill may still be a poor fit for the actual question the team must answer.
questionBank.distractorCoach: The trap is choosing a quality term that is true in general but not the main problem in this scenario.
questionBank.keyClue: Separate reliability, validity, relevance, bias, and duration before deciding which issue is primary.

questionBank.prompt: A test is reliable, relevant to the referral concern, and administered over an adequate period, but several items depend on unfamiliar cultural knowledge unrelated to the target skill. What remains problematic?
questionBank.why: Other quality features can be adequate while construct-irrelevant cultural demands still create unfairness.
questionBank.distractorCoach: The trap is choosing a quality term that is true in general but not the main problem in this scenario.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Separate reliability, validity, relevance, bias, and duration before deciding which issue is primary.

questionBank.prompt: Which sequence is best when evaluating a questionable assessment result?
options: Identify the concern, check measurement quality, compare with other relevant data, then decide whether more evidence is needed
Repeat the assessment under standardized conditions before reviewing any other evidence
Compare the result with one additional measure first, then decide whether the original result was valid
Collect additional data immediately before evaluating the quality of the evidence already available
questionBank.answer: Identify the concern, check measurement quality, compare with other relevant data, then decide whether more evidence is needed
questionBank.why: Sound evaluation considers the decision question, quality of the measure, and convergence across multiple relevant sources.
questionBank.distractorCoach: The trap is choosing a quality term that is true in general but not the main problem in this scenario.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Separate reliability, validity, relevance, bias, and duration before deciding which issue is primary.

questionBank.prompt: A parent requests access to the student's education records during a referral process. Which law most directly governs that request?
questionBank.why: FERPA protects education-record privacy and gives parents eligible rights to inspect records.
questionBank.distractorCoach: A complex stem may mention several laws; choose the one tied to the exact right or next action being asked about.
questionBank.keyClue: Separate privacy, access, educational benefit, and referral/evaluation responsibilities.

questionBank.prompt: A student with a disability cannot access required graphical information because no accessible alternative is provided. Which principle is most directly implicated?
questionBank.why: The barrier concerns equal access to the assessment, not confidentiality of records.
questionBank.distractorCoach: A complex stem may mention several laws; choose the one tied to the exact right or next action being asked about.
questionBank.keyClue: Separate privacy, access, educational benefit, and referral/evaluation responsibilities.

questionBank.prompt: A colleague says Rowley requires schools to maximize every student's potential. What is the strongest correction?
options: Rowley is associated with individualized educational benefit, not a maximize-potential standard
questionBank.answer: Rowley is associated with individualized educational benefit, not a maximize-potential standard
questionBank.why: The decision rejected a requirement to maximize potential and focused on appropriate educational benefit under the individualized program.
questionBank.distractorCoach: A complex stem may mention several laws; choose the one tied to the exact right or next action being asked about.
questionBank.keyClue: Separate privacy, access, educational benefit, and referral/evaluation responsibilities.

questionBank.prompt: A scenario mentions confidential records, disability access, and lack of progress. What should you do before selecting FERPA, ADA, or a referral principle?
options: Identify the specific legal or decision issue the question asks about
Choose ADA whenever disability is mentioned
Choose FERPA whenever school records exist
Choose referral whenever progress is low
questionBank.answer: Identify the specific legal or decision issue the question asks about
questionBank.why: Complex stems may contain several true facts. The task word and requested issue determine which principle controls.
questionBank.distractorCoach: A complex stem may mention several laws; choose the one tied to the exact right or next action being asked about.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Separate privacy, access, educational benefit, and referral/evaluation responsibilities.

questionBank.prompt: A student shows persistent lack of progress despite appropriate intervention, and the school psychologist identifies a suspected IDEA disability. Which next action is best supported?
options: Make a formal referral for special education evaluation
Wait indefinitely for another report card
questionBank.answer: Make a formal referral for special education evaluation
questionBank.why: Documented need plus suspected disability supports formal evaluation; eligibility and an IEP come after the appropriate evaluation process.
questionBank.distractorCoach: A complex stem may mention several laws; choose the one tied to the exact right or next action being asked about.
questionBank.transferReason: Requires applying the concept in a novel, mixed, or decision-based context rather than recalling a definition.
questionBank.keyClue: Separate privacy, access, educational benefit, and referral/evaluation responsibilities.

misconceptionCatalog.label: Reliability ↔ Validity
misconceptionCatalog.repair: Consistency does not prove the intended construct is measured.

misconceptionCatalog.label: Norm ↔ Criterion
misconceptionCatalog.repair: Norm = peers; criterion = a defined standard or skill.

misconceptionCatalog.label: Formative ↔ Informal
misconceptionCatalog.repair: Formative describes purpose; informal describes structure/method.

misconceptionCatalog.label: RTI ↔ Discrepancy
misconceptionCatalog.repair: RTI asks about response to intervention; discrepancy asks about the performance gap.

misconceptionCatalog.label: Bias ↔ Access
misconceptionCatalog.repair: Identify whether irrelevant background knowledge or inaccessible presentation creates the barrier.

misconceptionCatalog.label: FERPA ↔ ADA
misconceptionCatalog.repair: FERPA = education-record privacy; ADA = disability access/non-discrimination.

studySections.title: Assessment Methods
studySections.summary: Know what each assessment method actually does. Questions often gives you a classroom action and asks you to name the method.
rows: Document behavior or performance in context
Gather information directly from student, caregiver, or teacher
Collection of student work across time
Dated narrative note about an incident or behavior
Rate frequency, intensity, or degree using a set scale
studySections.trap: A narrative note is an anecdotal record. A predetermined frequency/intensity rating is a scaled checklist.

studySections.title: Assessment Purpose & Data
studySections.summary: Separate the purpose of an assessment from its format, and distinguish numerical from descriptive evidence.
rows: Ongoing feedback DURING learning used to adjust instruction
Numerical scores, frequency, percentages, cut scores
Frequent repeated measurement to evaluate response/growth
studySections.trap: Informal describes structure. Formative describes PURPOSE. Questions may place both in the same answer set.

studySections.title: Norm vs. Criterion
studySections.summary: Identify what the student's performance is being compared against.
rows: Performance compared with a peer/norm group
Performance compared with a defined standard, skill, or criterion
studySections.trap: Words such as national sample, percentile, or peers point to norm. Mastery, standard, benchmark, or defined performance level point to criterion.

studySections.title: Six Pre-Referral Steps
studySections.summary: Assessment scenarios often ask what happens NEXT. Memorize the sequence, then use the scenario clue rather than guessing.
rows: Problem is recognized, documented, and shared
Choose strategies/interventions and define the plan
Review effectiveness and adjust as needed
studySections.trap: Do not jump to implementation before the team has gathered information and developed a plan.

studySections.title: MTSS, RTI, SEL & PBIS
studySections.summary: Know the role of each framework/tool and what kind of problem it is designed to address.
rows: Broad multi-tiered system combining academic, behavioral, and other supports
Positive behavior support framework using prevention and data
Gap between expected and actual performance
Brief assessment to identify students at risk
Review existing evidence, identify gaps, then collect what is missing
studySections.trap: RTI asks how the learner responds to intervention. Discrepancy focuses on the performance gap.

studySections.title: Reliability, Validity, Relevance, Bias & Duration
studySections.summary: This is a high-yield discrimination set. Several answers can sound reasonable; identify the exact problem in the evidence.
rows: Does the measure assess the intended construct?
Does this evidence actually address THIS concern or decision?
Is an irrelevant factor unfairly influencing performance?
Was evidence collected across enough/appropriate time?
studySections.trap: Consistent results can still be invalid or irrelevant. First identify what the stem says is wrong: consistency, construct, fit, fairness, or time.

studySections.title: Law, Referral & Rowley
studySections.summary: Use the legal clue in the stem. Questions may combine privacy, access, referral, evaluation, and educational benefit in one answer set.
rows: Protects education-record privacy and access rights
Equal access and nondiscrimination for individuals with disabilities
Suspected disability affecting learning/participation should lead to appropriate evaluation
Documented lack of progress despite targeted interventions can support referral/evaluation
FAPE and an individualized program reasonably designed to provide educational benefit
studySections.trap: Do not delay an appropriate evaluation indefinitely just to keep trying interventions. Rowley is broader than one behavior strategy.

studySections.title: Multiple-Choice Strategy
studySections.summary: Your job is not to prove every option is false. Your job is to choose the option that MOST directly answers the exact question.
rows: Remove answers that answer a different question
Which option matches the exact course wording and scenario?
Do not change because an answer feels too easy
studySections.trap: When two answers are true in general, choose the one that is most directly supported by the scenario and the exact question asked.
